question: NPC: An array has a fixed length
intro: I'm Zoya, the Golem-Shaper. This chapter rebuilds your Python lists, dictionaries and classes in Java, one piece at a time. We start with the simplest container Java has.

steps.say: Java's simplest container is the **array**: a row of values, all of one type, whose **length** is fixed when it is made. `int[]` means an array of ints, and `new int[3]` makes one with three places, numbered 0 to 2, as in Python.

beats.say: Java's simplest container is the **array**: a row of values, all of one type, whose **length** is fixed when it is made.
beats.narrate: Java's simplest container is called an array. It's a row of values, all of the same type, and its length is fixed at the moment it's made.
Here, scores is made as a new array of three ints. Then two of its three places are filled: place 0, and place 2.

beats.say: `int[]` means an array of ints, and `new int[3]` makes one with three places, numbered 0 to 2, as in Python.
beats.narrate: The type, int followed by a pair of square brackets, means an array of ints. And new int, with a 3 in square brackets, makes one with three places, numbered 0 to 2, just as they would be in Python.

check.prompt: Place 1 was never set. What does `scores[1]` hold?
wrong: It stops the program when read
check.why: A new array of numbers starts full of zeros, so a place you never set holds 0.
check.narrate: Place 1 was never set. So what does scores, at place 1, hold?
check.why_narrate: A new array of numbers starts out full of zeros. So a place you never set still holds 0.

steps.say: You can also write the values out, much as you would a Python list. An array's length is `scores.length`, with no parentheses. Printed directly, an array shows a code, not its values. `Arrays.toString(scores)` builds the text `[90, 85, 77]`.

beats.say: You can also write the values out, much as you would a Python list. An array's length is `scores.length`, with no parentheses.
beats.narrate: You can also write the values out in full, much as you would for a Python list, but inside curly braces. And an array's length is scores dot length, with no parentheses after it.
Here the three values are written out in full. Then the program prints the length, which is 3, and the value at place 2, which is 77.

beats.code:
System.out.println(scores);                    // [I@1b6d3586
System.out.println(Arrays.toString(scores));   // [90, 85, 77]
beats.narrate: Now two ways to print the whole array. Compare what the comments say each line prints.

beats.say: Printed directly, an array shows a code, not its values. `Arrays.toString(scores)` builds the text `[90, 85, 77]`.
beats.narrate: Print an array directly, and you get a code, not its values. Arrays dot to string, handed scores, builds the text you wanted: 90, 85 and 77, in square brackets.

steps.say: Two Python habits fail here. An array cannot grow: there is no `append`. And there are no negative indexes: `scores[-1]` is not the last value.

beats.say: Two Python habits fail here. An array cannot grow: there is no `append`. And there are no negative indexes: `scores[-1]` is not the last value.
beats.narrate: Two Python habits fail here. First, an array can't grow: there's no append. Second, there are no negative indexes. Scores at minus 1 isn't the last value, the way it would be in Python.
Ask for place minus 1, and the program stops on that line with an array index out of bounds exception, much as Python stops with an index error for a place past the end.

outro: Your turn. A new array, the same rules.
intro_narrate: I'm Zoya, the Golem-Shaper. In this chapter we'll rebuild the lists, dictionaries and classes you made in Python, in Java, one piece at a time. And we'll start with the simplest container that Java has.
outro_narrate: Now it's your turn. Here's a new array, with the same rules.

question: This Java makes an array of four ints and sets two of its places. What does it print?
feedback: new int[4] makes four places, all starting at 0. hp[0] is never set, so it is still 0; hp[3] is 7 * 2 = 14; and hp.length is the number of places, 4, not the index of the last one.

question: In Python, marks[-1] is the last item. What happens when this Java runs?
code:
int[] marks = {4, 8, 15};
System.out.println(marks[-1]);
incorrect: It prints 15, counting back from the end of the array
It prints 4, wrapping round to the first value
javac refuses to compile it, as -1 is not a legal index
feedback: Java has no negative indexes. It checks every index when the line runs, and -1 is out of range, so the program stops there. javac does not look at index values ahead of time, so the file compiles. The last value is marks[marks.length - 1].

question: Declare gold as an array of 6 ints, made with new.
feedback: The type int[] says 'an array of ints', and new int[6] makes one with six places, each starting at 0. Java also accepts the older style int gold[], but int[] gold is the usual way to write it.

question: A Java array is made with new int[{{n}}]. What is the index of its last place?
feedback_template: Places are numbered from 0, so an array of length {{n}} has indexes 0 to {{expected}}. Its length is {{n}}; its last index is one less.

question: Printing an array directly shows a code such as [I@1b6d3586, not its values. Which line prints [4, 8, 15]?
code: int[] marks = {4, 8, 15};
incorrect: System.out.println(marks.toString());
System.out.println(String.join(marks));
System.out.println(marks.values());
feedback: An array has no toString of its own that lists its values, so println(marks) and marks.toString() both show its type, [I for an array of ints, then @ and a hash code in hexadecimal. Arrays.toString, from the class java.util.Arrays, builds the text [4, 8, 15]. String.join joins Strings, not ints, and an array has no values() method. An ArrayList, which comes next, prints its values with no help.

question: NPC: A list that can grow
intro: When the number of values changes as the program runs, an array is the wrong tool. Java has a list for that.

steps.say: An **ArrayList** is Java's version of the Python list: it grows as you add to it. Here is the same job in both languages. `<String>` says what the list holds, and every item must be a String. The empty `<>` on the right means the same type again. ArrayList lives in the package `java.util`, with HashMap, HashSet and Arrays. A file that uses them begins with `import java.util.*;`, or javac reports `cannot find symbol`.

beats.say: An **ArrayList** is Java's version of the Python list: it grows as you add to it. Here is the same job in both languages.
beats.narrate: An ArrayList is Java's version of the Python list. It grows as you add to it. Here's the same small job, done in both languages.

beats.code:
names = []
names.append("Ash")
names.append("Bog")
names[0] = "Elm"
print(names[1], len(names))
beats.narrate: First, the Python you know: an empty list, two appends, then place 0 is replaced, and the last line prints place 1 and the length.
And here's the Java. Line by line, it does the same job. Compare the two, one line at a time.

beats.say: `<String>` says what the list holds, and every item must be a String. The empty `<>` on the right means the same type again.
beats.narrate: The word String, in angle brackets, says what this list holds, and every item in it must be a String. The empty angle brackets on the right just mean: the same type again.

beats.say: ArrayList lives in the package `java.util`, with HashMap, HashSet and Arrays. A file that uses them begins with `import java.util.*;`, or javac reports `cannot find symbol`.
beats.narrate: ArrayList lives in a package called java dot util, along with HashMap, HashSet and Arrays. So a file that uses them begins with the line import java dot util dot star. Leave it out, and javac reports that it cannot find symbol.

steps.say: The operations are renamed. `append` becomes `add`, reading `names[i]` becomes `names.get(i)`, `len(names)` becomes `names.size()`, and `x in names` becomes `names.contains(x)`. `names.insert(i, x)` becomes `names.add(i, x)`: given a position, `add` puts the new item there and pushes the rest along.

beats.say: The operations are renamed. `append` becomes `add`, reading `names[i]` becomes `names.get(i)`, `len(names)` becomes `names.size()`, and `x in names` becomes `names.contains(x)`.
beats.narrate: The operations are just renamed. Append becomes add. Reading names at i becomes names dot get i. Len of names becomes names dot size. And x in names becomes names dot contains x.

beats.say: `names.insert(i, x)` becomes `names.add(i, x)`: given a position, `add` puts the new item there and pushes the rest along.
beats.narrate: And Python's insert becomes add, with a position. Given a position, add puts the new item there, and pushes the rest along by one.

check.why: Changing a place is `set`. `add(1, "Fen")` would insert a new item at place 1 and push the rest along, leaving the old item in the list. Square brackets work only on arrays.
check.narrate: How does Java write Python's names at 1 equals Fen?
check.why_narrate: Changing a place is set. Add, with a position, would insert a new item at place 1, and push the others along, so the old item would still be in the list. And square brackets only work on arrays.

steps.say: A **for-each loop** walks through a list as Python's `for` does. You write the type of each item in front of its name. Printed whole, an ArrayList shows its items in square brackets, without quotation marks.

beats.say: A **for-each loop** walks through a list as Python's `for` does. You write the type of each item in front of its name.
beats.narrate: A for-each loop walks through a list the way Python's for loop does. The one difference: you write the type of each item in front of its name.
Read the colon as the word in. For each String n in names, print n. And the last line prints the whole list at once.

beats.say: Printed whole, an ArrayList shows its items in square brackets, without quotation marks.
beats.narrate: When you print a whole ArrayList, it shows its items in square brackets, like a Python list, but without any quotation marks around the strings.

outro: Now match each Python habit to its Java spelling.

outro_narrate: Now it's your turn. Match each Python habit to the way Java spells it.

question: Match each Python list operation to the ArrayList code that does the same.
feedback: add for append, get and set for reading and changing a place, size for len, add with a position for insert, and contains for in. Square brackets belong to arrays only.

question: This ArrayList is added to and changed. What does it print?
feedback: add(0, "map") inserts at the front, pushing rope and lamp along: [map, rope, lamp]. set(2, "salt") then replaces place 2, the lamp, giving [map, rope, salt]. So place 1 is rope, place 2 is salt, and size() is 3.

question: Each of these asks for its size in its own way. Match each one to the code that gives its size.
feedback: An array's length is a field, so it has no parentheses. A String's length() is a method, so it does. Collections such as ArrayList use size(). Python asks all three with len.

incorrect: String first = names.get(0);

question: words is an ArrayList<String>. Which Java loop does the same as this Python?
code:
for w in words:
    print(w)
incorrect: for (w in words) { System.out.println(w); }

question: A Java {{1}} has a length fixed when it is made, read as scores.{{2}} with no parentheses. An {{3}} grows as you add to it, and names.{{4}}() says how many items it holds.
feedback: Fixed length: an array, whose length is a field (scores.length). Growing: an ArrayList, whose size() is a method. Mixing the two up, writing scores.size() or names.length, is an error javac reports as 'cannot find symbol'.

question: NPC: Why Integer, not int
intro: Try to make a list of whole numbers the obvious way, and Java refuses. Here is why, and what to write instead.

steps.say: A collection holds **objects**. An `int` is not an object but a bare value, which Java calls a **primitive type**. So each primitive type has a **wrapper class** that holds one such value as an object: `Integer` for `int`, `Double` for `double`, `Boolean` for `boolean`, and `Character` for `char`.

beats.code:
ArrayList<int> scores = new ArrayList<>();       // error
ArrayList<Integer> scores = new ArrayList<>();   // fine
beats.narrate: Two lines. The first asks for a list of int, and javac refuses it. The second asks for a list of Integer, with a capital I, and that's fine.

beats.say: A collection holds **objects**. An `int` is not an object but a bare value, which Java calls a **primitive type**.
beats.narrate: A collection holds objects. And an int isn't an object. It's a bare value, which Java calls a primitive type.

beats.say: So each primitive type has a **wrapper class** that holds one such value as an object: `Integer` for `int`, `Double` for `double`, `Boolean` for `boolean`, and `Character` for `char`.
beats.narrate: So each primitive type has a wrapper class, which holds one such value as an object. Integer for int, Double for double, Boolean for boolean, and Character for char.

steps.say: You rarely see the wrapping. Java wraps an `int` into an `Integer` as it goes into a list, which is called **autoboxing**, and unwraps it as it comes out, called **unboxing**.

beats.say: You rarely see the wrapping. Java wraps an `int` into an `Integer` as it goes into a list, which is called **autoboxing**, and unwraps it as it comes out, called **unboxing**.
beats.narrate: You rarely see the wrapping happen. Java wraps an int into an Integer as it goes into a list, which is called autoboxing. And it unwraps it again as it comes out, which is called unboxing.
So you add a plain 90, and read it back into a plain int called first. Now look at what the last line does with it.

check.prompt: What does the last line print?
check.why: `first` is a plain `int` again, so `+ 5` is arithmetic: 95.
check.narrate: So what does the last line print?
check.why_narrate: First is a plain int again, after unboxing. So plus 5 is ordinary arithmetic, and it prints 95.

steps.say: One trap. On an `ArrayList<Integer>`, `nums.remove(1)` removes the item at **position** 1, not the value 1. To remove a value, hand `remove` an `Integer` object, made with `Integer.valueOf`.

beats.say: One trap. On an `ArrayList<Integer>`, `nums.remove(1)` removes the item at **position** 1, not the value 1.
beats.narrate: Here's the one trap. On a list of Integers, nums dot remove 1 removes the item at position 1. Not the value 1, the way Python's remove would.
Follow the comments. The first remove takes out position 1, which holds the 20. The second hands remove an Integer object, so it removes the value 1.

beats.say: To remove a value, hand `remove` an `Integer` object, made with `Integer.valueOf`.
beats.narrate: So, to remove a value rather than a position, hand remove an Integer object, made with Integer dot value of.

intro_narrate: Try to make a list of whole numbers in the obvious way, and Java refuses. Let me show you why, and what to write instead.
outro_narrate: Now it's your turn. Trace one yourself.

feedback: remove(0) is given an int, so it removes position 0, the 7, leaving [3, 0]. remove(Integer.valueOf(0)) is given an Integer object, so it removes the value 0, leaving [3].

feedback: Each Integer is unboxed into the int m, so the loop is an ordinary search for the largest: best ends at 9. marks.get(1) is 5, and both sides of + are numbers, so it adds: 9 + 5 = 14.

incorrect: ArrayList<int> d = new ArrayList<>();
ArrayList<double> e = new ArrayList<>();
ArrayList<Integer> f = {1, 2, 3};
feedback: The type in angle brackets has to be a class, such as Integer, Character, Double or String. int and double are primitive types, so they are refused there. And {1, 2, 3} works only for an array: javac calls it an illegal initializer for an ArrayList, which is filled with add.

question: Why does javac refuse ArrayList<int>?
correct: A collection holds objects, and an int is a primitive value, not an object
incorrect: An ArrayList stores every item as text, so numbers have to be converted first

feedback: Most wrapper classes are the primitive's name with a capital letter: Double for double, Boolean for boolean. The two that differ are Integer for int and Character for char.

question: NPC: A dictionary becomes a HashMap
intro: Your dictionaries and sets come with you too. Their names change, and so does one promise a Python dictionary makes.

steps.say: Java's dictionary is the **HashMap**. Its type names two things: the type of its **keys**, then the type of its **values**. `put` stores a value under a key, replacing any value already there, and `get` reads it.

beats.say: Java's dictionary is the **HashMap**. Its type names two things: the type of its **keys**, then the type of its **values**.
beats.narrate: Java's dictionary is called a HashMap. Its type names two things: first the type of its keys, and then the type of its values.

beats.code:
stock = {}
stock["rope"] = 3
stock["lamp"] = 1
print(stock["rope"])
beats.narrate: Here's a Python dictionary of how many of each thing is in stock: rope, and a lamp. Then it prints the rope.
And the same in Java. The keys are Strings, and the values are Integers. Storing is put, and reading is get.

beats.say: `put` stores a value under a key, replacing any value already there, and `get` reads it.
beats.narrate: Put stores a value under a key, and replaces any value that's already there. Get reads it back.

steps.say: A missing key is where the two differ. Python's `stock["salt"]` stops the program with a KeyError.

beats.say: A missing key is where the two differ. Python's `stock["salt"]` stops the program with a KeyError.
beats.narrate: A missing key is where the two differ. In Python, stock at salt, when there's no salt, stops the program with a key error.

check.prompt: What does Java's `stock.get("salt")` give, when there is no salt?
check.why: `get` returns **null**, Java's word for no object at all, like Python's `None`. Put that `null` into an `int`, and the program stops with a **NullPointerException**.
check.narrate: So what does Java's stock dot get salt give you, when there's no salt?
check.why_narrate: Get returns null. That's Java's word for no object at all, much like Python's None. And if you put that null into an int, the program stops, with a null pointer exception.

steps.say: For Python's `in` and `get` with a default, Java has `containsKey` and `getOrDefault`.

beats.say: For Python's `in` and `get` with a default, Java has `containsKey` and `getOrDefault`.
beats.narrate: And for Python's in, and Python's get with a default, Java has contains key, and get or default.

beats.code:
System.out.println(stock.containsKey("salt"));       // false
System.out.println(stock.getOrDefault("salt", 0));   // 0
beats.narrate: Contains key, asking for salt, prints false. And get or default, asking for salt with 0 as the default, prints 0.

steps.say: One promise changes. A Python dictionary keeps its keys in the order you added them. A HashMap promises no order: printed or looped over, its keys come out in an order of its own. Python's set is Java's **HashSet**: no duplicates, no promised order, and `add` returns `false` when the item was already there.

beats.say: One promise changes. A Python dictionary keeps its keys in the order you added them. A HashMap promises no order: printed or looped over, its keys come out in an order of its own.
beats.narrate: One promise changes. A Python dictionary keeps its keys in the order you added them. A HashMap promises no order at all. Print it, or loop over it, and its keys come out in an order of its own.

beats.say: Python's set is Java's **HashSet**: no duplicates, no promised order, and `add` returns `false` when the item was already there.
beats.narrate: And Python's set is Java's HashSet. It holds no duplicates, it promises no order, and its add method returns false when the item was already there.
The first add of fox returns true. The second returns false, because fox is already in the set, so nothing is added.

question: Put the lines in order so that the program stores 2 ropes, adds 3 more, and prints ten times the total: 50.

question: add on a HashSet returns true or false. What does it print?
feedback: add returns true when it adds the item and false when the item was already there. The second fox is refused, so again is false and the set holds two items: a set keeps no duplicates.

question: A Python dictionary keeps its keys in the order they were added. What can you count on about the order of a HashMap's keys?
correct: No particular order: it may differ from the order you added them
incorrect: The order the keys were added, the same as in a Python dictionary
Alphabetical order, since the keys are sorted as they are stored
The reverse of the order added, as the newest key goes in first

correct: It stops with a NullPointerException: there is no Integer to unwrap
incorrect: n is set to 0, the value an int starts with before anything is stored

question: Python's dictionary becomes Java's {{1}}, and Python's set becomes Java's {{2}}. Where Python stops with a KeyError, get on a map gives {{3}}.
feedback: A HashMap maps keys to values, a HashSet holds items with no duplicates, and neither promises an order. A missing key gives null, Java's 'no object at all'.

question: NPC: A list of dictionaries becomes a list of objects
intro: In Python you kept records as a list of dictionaries. Java has a better tool for that job, and you already know it from Python: a class.

steps.say: A Java map gives all its values one type, so a name and an hp cannot each keep a type of their own.

beats.code:
party = [
    {"name": "Ayla", "hp": 30},
    {"name": "Bren", "hp": 12},
]
print(party[1]["hp"])
beats.narrate: Here's the shape you know from Python: a list of two dictionaries, one for each hero, each with a name and an hp. The last line reads the second hero's hp.

beats.say: A Java map gives all its values one type, so a name and an hp cannot each keep a type of their own.
beats.narrate: A Java map gives all of its values one single type. So a name and an hp can't each keep a type of their own, the way they could in the Python dictionary.

steps.say: So each record becomes an object, and the dictionary's keys become the class's **fields**, each with its type.

beats.say: So each record becomes an object, and the dictionary's keys become the class's **fields**, each with its type.
beats.narrate: So instead, each record becomes an object. And the dictionary's keys become the class's fields, each declared with its own type.
Here's the class Hero. The two fields, name and hp, are declared at the top. Below them is the code that sets up each new hero. We'll come back to that part soon, and look at it closely.
And here's the party: an ArrayList of Hero objects. Two heroes are added, and the last line reads the second hero's hp.

check.why_narrate: Get 0 gives you the Hero at place 0. Then dot name reads that hero's field. A Hero is an object, not a map, so it has no get method of its own.

steps.say: The keys are now decided in advance, and javac checks every use of them before the program runs. Python's `party[1]["hpp"]` would run up to that line, and only then stop, with a KeyError.

beats.say: The keys are now decided in advance, and javac checks every use of them before the program runs.
beats.narrate: The keys are now decided in advance, as fields. So javac checks every use of them, before the program ever runs.

beats.say: Python's `party[1]["hpp"]` would run up to that line, and only then stop, with a KeyError.
beats.narrate: In Python, party at 1, at h p p, would run happily right up to that line, and only then stop, with a key error.

intro_narrate: In Python, you kept records as a list of dictionaries, one dictionary for each record. Java has a better tool for that job, and you already know it from Python: a class.

question: NPC: Packages, and where the files go

steps.say: A **package** is a named group of classes. A file names its package in its very first line. By convention, package names begin with a domain name written backwards, such as `com.example.game`. Each company owns its domain, so its packages do not clash with another company's. The folders mirror the package, one for each part of its name: this file goes in `guild/items/Potion.java`, and its compiled `Potion.class` in a `guild/items` folder too. That is where Java's tools look for a class they need. A file with no package line, like every one so far, is in the **unnamed package**.

Yes: test code may call any method
feedback: Access goes by package, not by folder. Both files declare package guild.items, so they are in one package, even though one sits under src/main/java and the other under src/test/java. That is why tests are put in the same package as the code they test: they can reach its package-private parts. A private method would still be out of reach.

prompt: Shop.java is in src/main/java/guild/shop; Potion.java is in src/main/java/guild/items. Complete Shop.java.
feedback: Below src/main/java, each folder is one part of a package name, and the parts are joined with dots: the folder guild/shop is the package guild.shop. Shop names its own package on its first line, and imports Potion by its full name, its package and then the class.

question: Game.java, in the package guild, uses Potion from guild.items but has no import line. What does javac report?
incorrect: package guild.items does not exist
Potion is not public in guild.items
missing import for class Potion
feedback: Without the import, javac looks for Potion in Game's own package, guild, finds nothing, and cannot find the symbol. import guild.items.Potion; tells it where to look. 'package guild.items does not exist' is what you see when the import is there but the package's folder is not where javac looks.

question: By convention, package names begin with a domain name written backwards, as in com.example.game. Why?
correct: A company owns its domain, so its package names are its own
incorrect: Java downloads each class from the website the domain names
javac checks that whoever compiles it owns that domain
It makes the package public, so that other companies may use it
feedback: A domain name has one owner, so starting package names with it, reversed so that the most general part comes first, keeps one company's packages apart from another's: com.example.game.Potion and org.guild.Potion are different classes. It is a convention only: nothing is downloaded, javac checks no ownership, and the name says nothing about access.

question: Write this Python function in Java. The numbers now come in an int array.
hint: Declare the total as an int, set to 0, before the loop. A for-each loop reads each number: for (int n : nums).
feedback: The accumulator pattern, in Java: declare the total and set it to 0 before the loop, add inside, return after. The for-each loop works on an array just as on a list, naming each item's type.

question: Write this Python function in Java. words is now an ArrayList<String>.
signature: public int countLong(ArrayList<String> words, int minLen)
hint: len(w) becomes w.length(), with parentheses, since a String's length is a method.
feedback: A counter with a condition: start at 0, add one for each word that passes the test, return after the loop. A String's length() is a method; an array's length is a field.

question: Python builds this list in one line, with a comprehension. Java has no comprehensions: write the loop that builds the new list, and return it.
code:
def evens(nums):
    return [n for n in nums if n % 2 == 0]
hint: Make an empty ArrayList<Integer> first, add each even number to it inside a for-each loop, then return it.
feedback: A comprehension is a loop in one line. Written out, it is: make an empty list, loop, add the items that pass the test, return the list. The original list is left as it was.

question: Write this Python counting function in Java. It returns a HashMap from each word to the number of times it appears.
hint: counts.get(w, 0) becomes counts.getOrDefault(w, 0), and counts[w] = ... becomes counts.put(w, ...).
feedback: The counting pattern: read the count so far, with 0 for a word not seen yet, add one, and store it back. getOrDefault is what keeps a new word from giving null.

question: Write this Python function in Java, with a HashSet in place of the Python set.
hint: item in seen becomes seen.contains(item), and Python's True and False are written true and false.
feedback: Remember what has been seen in a set, and stop as soon as an item is already there. Since add returns false for an item already in the set, if (!seen.add(item)) return true; does the check and the adding in one line.

question: Write heal in Java. It raises THIS hero's hp by amount, but never above maxHp. The Python version is shown.
hint: Inside the class, the fields are used by their plain names, hp and maxHp. Java needs no self.
feedback: A method changes the fields of the object it was called on. Python writes self.hp every time; Java lets you write hp, and this.hp means the same. Add first, then pull hp back down to maxHp if it went over.

question: Write totalHp in Java: the hp of every hero in THIS party, added up. A Hero's hp is private, so read it with getHp().

tests.run:
Party p = new Party();
p.add(new Hero("Cass", 7));

hint: Loop over the field heroes with for (Hero h : heroes), and add h.getHp() to a total.
feedback: An object that holds a list of other objects: the loop walks the Party's own list, and each Hero is asked for its hp through its getter, because the field itself is private to Hero. h.hp would not compile here.

question: Write the whole class Potion, with its data hidden. Private fields: String name, int power. A constructor, Potion(String name, int power), that stores both. A getter, public int getPower(). A public String toString() that returns the name and then the power in brackets, as in Ember (40).

tests.run:
Potion a = new Potion("Frost", 25);
Potion b = new Potion("Mist", 5);

hint: Four parts, in order: the two private fields, the constructor, the getter, and toString. A constructor has the class's name and no return type.
feedback: The whole chapter in one class: fields declared with their types and hidden with private, a constructor in place of __init__, a public getter as the one way in, and toString in place of __str__, so the object prints as text.
